templates.description: A minor piece was left briefly undefended early in the opening.
templates.text: After {played}, {piece} on {square} was briefly loose. Get in the habit of checking every piece after you move it.

templates.description: A developing piece walked into a pin worth real tempo.
templates.text: {played} let your opponent pin {piece} to something more valuable. Break the pin quickly or you will keep losing tempo.

templates.description: An early fork wins a piece outright, a costly opening blunder.
templates.text: {played} walked straight into a fork; {best_move} was already winning a piece back. You gave up {swing} in a handful of moves.

templates.description: A piece hangs in the opening for a real material loss.
templates.text: {played} leaves {piece} hanging for real material. {best_move} kept it defended and kept your development on track.

templates.description: A piece hangs outright in the opening for a costly blunder.
templates.text: {played} hangs {piece} outright this early. You gave up {swing} for a piece that had a safe square available.

templates.description: A fork in the opening wins material at a real cost.
templates.text: {played} walks into a fork that wins material back for your opponent. {best_move} kept your pieces out of the double attack.

templates.description: A pin in the opening costs a piece outright.
templates.text: {played} lets your opponent pin {piece} and win it outright. That single pin cost you {swing} before move fifteen.

templates.description: A piece was left loosely defended for a move or two.
templates.text: {piece} on {square} was only loosely defended after {played}. A quick defender check before you move keeps this from becoming a real loss.

templates.description: A piece shift opened a discovered attack worth a small edge.
templates.text: Moving {piece} opened a discovered attack you did not need to allow. Watch what lines open up before you move a piece off its file or diagonal.

templates.description: One defender was covering two jobs it could not both do.
templates.text: {piece} on {square} was covering two things at once, and {played} asked too much of it. Find the piece with the least to do before you rely on it.

templates.description: A trade removed the one defender your position needed.
templates.text: {played} traded off the piece defending {target_square}, which was the whole point of the trade for your opponent. Before trading, ask what the piece you are removing was actually doing.

templates.description: A skewer forced a bigger piece to move and lose material.
templates.text: {played} lined your pieces up for a skewer along that file. {best_move} kept them apart and stayed level.

templates.description: The back rank was undefended and cost material or worse.
templates.text: {played} left your back rank open with no escape square for the king. You gave up {swing} to a threat a single luft move would have stopped.

templates.description: A short mating attack was already on the board and missed.
templates.text: {played} missed a forced mating idea sitting on the board. {best_move} was already ending the game in your favor.

templates.description: A piece was already trapped with no safe square to reach.
templates.text: {piece} on {square} had no safe square left after {played}. That cost you {swing} for a piece that was already lost.

templates.description: A piece hangs in the middlegame for a real material loss.
templates.text: {played} leaves {piece} on {square} hanging in the middle of the game. {best_move} kept it defended.

templates.description: A piece hangs outright in the middlegame for a costly blunder.
templates.text: {played} hangs {piece} outright in the middlegame. You gave up {swing} for a piece that had a safe square.

templates.description: A fork in the middlegame wins material at a real cost.
templates.text: {played} allows a fork that wins material back in the middlegame. {best_move} kept your pieces apart and out of the double attack.

templates.description: A fork in the middlegame wins material outright, a costly blunder.
templates.text: {played} walks straight into a fork that wins material outright. You gave up {swing} to a double attack you could have avoided.

templates.description: A pin in the middlegame costs real material or tempo.
templates.text: {played} lets your opponent pin {piece} to something more valuable. {best_move} kept the pin from ever landing.

templates.description: A pin in the middlegame costs a piece outright.
templates.text: {played} lets your opponent pin {piece} and win it outright in the middlegame. That cost you {swing} in a few moves.

templates.description: A piece was briefly undefended in a simplified position.
templates.text: With so few pieces left, {piece} on {square} needed a second look after {played}. In the endgame every undefended unit is easy for your opponent to spot.

templates.description: A king and pawn fork picked up material in a simple ending.
templates.text: {played} allowed a fork that picks off a pawn in an ending where every pawn matters. {best_move} kept your structure intact.

templates.description: A skewer in the ending forced the loss of the deciding piece.
templates.text: {played} put your king and rook on the same line for a skewer. You gave up {swing} in a position that should have been holdable.

templates.description: A pin in the ending stopped the one piece that could defend.
templates.text: {played} pinned your only active defender to the king. That let the position slip by {swing} in a few moves.

templates.description: A small tactical slip happened without one single clear cause.
templates.text: {played} gives up a little ground here. {best_move} kept the position tighter.

templates.description: A concrete tactical loss happened without one single clear reason.
templates.text: {played} gave up {swing}. {best_move} kept things under control; compare the two before your next move.

templates.description: A significant tactical loss happened without one single clear reason.
templates.text: {played} gave up {swing} here. {best_move} was the safer path; take a moment to compare the lines next time.

templates.description: A slightly passive setup ceded central space early on.
templates.text: {played} let your opponent claim more central space than they should have gotten for free. A central pawn break soon will help you contest it back.

templates.description: Castling was delayed while the center opened up around the king.
templates.text: {played} put off castling while the center was opening up. {best_move} tucked your king away before the position got sharp.

templates.description: A piece was misplaced badly enough to cost real activity.
templates.text: {played} sent {piece} somewhere it will need several moves to escape from. That kind of lost tempo is worth {swing} against a player who develops normally.

templates.description: A pawn move created a hole for an enemy piece to use.
templates.text: {played} left a hole on {square} that a well-placed piece can now sit on. Try to cover that square or trade off the piece heading for it.

templates.description: A trade left an isolated pawn without enough compensation.
templates.text: {played} settled for an isolated pawn without the activity to make up for it. Keep your pieces active enough to justify the weakness, or avoid the trade next time.

templates.description: An open file was handed to your opponent without a fight.
templates.text: {played} gave up the open file instead of contesting it. {best_move} put a rook there first and kept the file for you.

templates.description: A trade simplified into an ending your side gains less from.
templates.text: {played} traded pieces off in a position where you needed them on the board. Keep tension when the resulting endgame favors your opponent's structure.

templates.description: The king's pawn shield was loosened for no clear gain.
templates.text: {played} pushed a pawn shielding your king without a concrete reason to. {best_move} kept the shelter intact while making progress elsewhere.

templates.description: A trade left a piece passive for the rest of the game.
templates.text: {played} left you with a piece that has almost nothing to do for the rest of the game. That kind of imbalance is worth {swing} even without a single tactic.

templates.description: A permanent hole was created right next to your own king.
templates.text: {played} put a permanent hole on {square}, right where your king lives. A piece is going to plant itself there and you have no pawn left to remove it.

templates.description: The king was opened to a live attack with pieces still on.
templates.text: {played} opened lines toward your own king while your opponent still has attackers on the board. You gave up {swing} to an attack a safer move would have avoided.

templates.description: A pawn move fixed a weakness for the rest of the game.
templates.text: {played} fixed your pawn structure in a shape that is easy to attack. In a simplified position, structure decides more than any single move.

templates.description: A trade removed the one piece stopping the opposing plan.
templates.text: {played} traded off the piece keeping your opponent's plan in check. {best_move} kept it on the board and kept you in the fight.

templates.description: A rook sat idle instead of fighting for the open file.
templates.text: {played} left your rook stuck behind pawns instead of finding the open file. That passivity cost {swing} in a position that needed your rook active.

templates.description: A passive move let the opponent's pieces take over the board.
templates.text: {played} kept your pieces on their starting squares while your opponent's took over the board. You gave up {swing} to activity alone.

templates.description: A small positional slip happened without one single sharp cause.
templates.text: {played} gives up a small amount of ground. {best_move} kept your position more comfortable.

templates.description: A positional mistake cost ground without one single sharp cause.
templates.text: {played} costs you {swing} in this position. {best_move} was the sturdier choice.

templates.description: A serious positional loss happened without one single sharp cause.
templates.text: {played} costs you {swing} here. {best_move} kept your position together; worth comparing the two moves.

templates.description: The king stayed passive when it needed to join the fight.
templates.text: {played} kept your king at home instead of marching it toward the action. In the endgame your king is a fighting piece, and every tempo centralizing it matters.

templates.description: The opposition was given up a move before it was needed.
templates.text: {played} let go of the opposition a move earlier than you had to. {best_move} kept the key squares and kept the result in hand.

templates.description: A passed pawn was left unsupported and easy to round up.
templates.text: {played} pushed the passed pawn without an escort, so it never got far. {best_move} brought a piece along first and kept the pawn's value.

templates.description: The rook was placed in front of the pawn instead of behind it.
templates.text: {played} put your rook in front of the pawn instead of behind it. A rook belongs behind a passed pawn, yours or your opponent's.

templates.description: A winning edge slipped to equal by allowing counterplay.
templates.text: {played} allowed exactly the counterplay a winning position needs to avoid. You gave up {swing} converting an advantage that should have been routine.

templates.description: The king stayed a move behind in a race the kings decided.
templates.text: {played} left your king a full move behind in a race decided by tempo alone. That cost {swing} in a position your king could have contested.

templates.description: A small technical slip in the ending cost a little ground.
templates.text: {played} gives up a little in this ending. {best_move} was the more precise choice.

templates.description: A technical error in the ending cost real ground.
templates.text: {played} costs you {swing} in this ending. {best_move} kept your technique on track.

templates.description: A serious technical error in the ending cost real ground.
templates.text: {played} costs you {swing} in this ending. {best_move} was the move that kept everything under control.

templates.description: A natural developing move was skipped for something slower.
templates.text: {played} spends a move on something other than development this early. {best_move} brings a piece out and keeps pace with known theory.

templates.description: The same piece moved twice before development was finished.
templates.text: {played} moves a piece a second time while others stay home. Finish developing before you go hunting for something extra.

templates.description: A known opening line was left for an untested idea too early.
templates.text: {played} steps outside known theory earlier than the position calls for. {best_move} keeps you in a well-tested line with a clear plan.

templates.description: An opening principle was broken badly enough to lose real ground.
templates.text: {played} breaks a basic opening principle and it costs you right away. You gave up {swing} before move fifteen.

templates.description: The queen came out too early and ran into an attack.
templates.text: {played} brings your queen out before your other pieces are ready to support it. Chasing it around cost {swing} in tempo alone.

templates.description: A small opening slip cost a little ground early on.
templates.text: {played} gives up a small amount of ground this early. {best_move} kept you closer to known theory.

templates.description: An opening error cost real ground early in the game.
templates.text: {played} costs you {swing} this early in the game. {best_move} was the steadier choice.

templates.description: A serious opening error cost real ground early in the game.
templates.text: {played} costs you {swing} this early. {best_move} was the move that kept your position solid.

templates.description: A decent move was played too fast with time to spare.
templates.text: {played} came out fast even though your clock had plenty left. Slowing down on non-forced moves usually costs less than the time you save.

templates.description: A rushed move under time pressure missed a better option.
templates.text: {played} was a fast choice with the clock getting low. {best_move} was available and worth the extra seconds to find.

templates.description: A low clock led to a move that loses material outright.
templates.text: {played} came under real time pressure and it cost {swing}. When the clock is low, a shorter, safer move beats a fast, risky one.

templates.description: A short forcing line was calculated one move too shallow.
templates.text: {played} stops calculating the line one move too early. Push the forcing sequence one move further before you commit to it.

templates.description: A forcing sequence was seen but its final point was missed.
templates.text: {played} follows the right idea but stops one move short of the point. The point of the line is {line}; carry your calculation that far next time.

templates.description: A deep line was miscalculated and the position was lost.
templates.text: {played} misjudges the end of a forcing line several moves deep. That miscalculation cost {swing} in a sequence you had already started.

templates.description: The engine flags a small loss with no clear reason.
templates.text: {played} loses a little ground here for reasons that are not clear-cut. Keep an eye on this type of position in review.

templates.description: The error does not fit a single clear pattern this time.
templates.text: {played} costs you some ground without an obvious single cause. {best_move} was the more solid choice in this position.

templates.description: A real loss happened with no single, obvious explanation.
templates.text: {played} gave up {swing} here for reasons that do not reduce to one clean explanation. Positions like this are worth a closer look after the game.

templates.description: A normal, timely developing move that keeps pace with theory.
templates.text: {played} is a solid developing move that keeps your plan on track. Keep bringing pieces out before you look for anything sharper.

templates.description: A move that claims central space at the right moment.
templates.text: {played} grabs central space while your opponent is still getting organized. That kind of space is easy to use and hard to give back.

templates.description: Castling early keeps the king safe before the position sharpens.
templates.text: {played} gets your king to safety before things get complicated. That is exactly the right moment for it.

templates.description: A tactic was found and calculated correctly to the end.
templates.text: {played} finds the fork and follows it through to the end. That is a sharp piece of calculation.

templates.description: A piece was rerouted to a clearly better square.
templates.text: {played} sends {piece} to a square where it finally has something to do. Small improvements like that add up over a game.

templates.description: A rook claimed the open file before the opponent could.
templates.text: {played} gets your rook to the open file first. That file is yours to use for the rest of the middlegame.

templates.description: The king was activated at exactly the right moment.
templates.text: {played} brings your king into the game right when it matters most. That kind of king activity often decides simple endings.

templates.description: A passed pawn was pushed with the right support behind it.
templates.text: {played} pushes the passed pawn with a piece already backing it up. That is the technique that turns an edge into a full point.

templates.description: Textbook rook placement made a technical ending straightforward.
templates.text: {played} puts your rook exactly where rook endgame technique says it belongs. Positions like this are won by technique, not tricks.

templates.description: The strongest move in the position, found and played.
templates.text: {played} is the strongest move here. Well calculated.

templates.description: The most resilient defense in a difficult position was found.
templates.text: {played} is the toughest defense available in a hard spot. That kind of resourcefulness saves games that look lost.

templates.description: A clean, accurate move kept a winning position fully under control.
templates.text: {played} keeps everything under control without giving your opponent any chances. That is how winning positions stay winning.

templates.description: An ordinary book move that keeps the position balanced.
templates.text: {played} is a normal, well-known move here. Nothing special is required of you yet.

templates.description: A quiet move that neither gains nor gives up central ground.
templates.text: {played} keeps things level in the center without committing to much. A perfectly fine, unremarkable choice.

templates.description: A solid, standard setup move with nothing sharp about it.
templates.text: {played} keeps your position solid without taking on any risk. Plenty of games are won from positions just like this one.

templates.description: A reasonable move that keeps your pieces about where they were.
templates.text: {played} is a fine, ordinary move that keeps your position together. No theme stands out here either way.

templates.description: A trade that changes little about the shape of the position.
templates.text: {played} trades a pair of pieces without changing much about the position. Either recapture would have kept things about the same.

templates.description: A pawn move that keeps the structure flexible without weakening it.
templates.text: {played} keeps your pawn structure flexible for now. There is no clear commitment here yet, which is fine.

templates.description: A standard king move that keeps the position from changing much.
templates.text: {played} keeps the kings roughly where they were. This kind of ending can stay balanced for a while yet.

templates.description: A rook move that keeps the position about where it was.
templates.text: {played} keeps your rook active without changing the balance of the position. A perfectly reasonable waiting move.

templates.description: A steady king step keeps options open in a level ending.
templates.text: {played} brings your king a step closer to the action without committing to a plan yet. That keeps your options open.

templates.description: An ordinary move that does not change the evaluation much either way.
templates.text: {played} is a reasonable move that does not shift the evaluation much. Nothing here needs your attention right now.

templates.description: A quick, simple decision that used a normal amount of time.
templates.text: {played} took about the time you would expect for a move like this. Your clock management here was fine.

templates.description: A safe, solid choice in a position that is not yet critical.
templates.text: {played} is a safe choice in a position that has not become sharp yet. There is no pressing reason to look for more.
